clue.text: Maybe what Drake chose to follow principal part of meal

definitions.text: Maybe what Drake chose to follow
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a route across the Spanish Main, the Caribbean waters where Drake sailed
second meaning: the central dish of a dinner, after the starter

explanation.walkthrough: The Main was the old name for the sea around the Spanish colonies in the Caribbean, which Sir Francis Drake raided; a course is the line a ship follows. 'Maybe' flags the playful reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The biggest dish served during dinner is called by this phrase, the entree that follows any starter.

clue.text: Bond's boss initially ignores Moneypenny's exasperated gesture

parts.note: M heads the secret service in the James Bond stories

indicators.note: something done initially happens at the start, so only the opening letter of each following word is used

parts.note: the opening letters of three consecutive words

explanation.surface: Bond's chief pretends not to notice his secretary Moneypenny rolling her eyes at him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exasperated gesture' reads as one phrase, but 'exasperated' only supplies its first letter and 'gesture' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To act something out silently with movements of the hands and body is to communicate by wordless signs.

clue.text: Gets pub fruit drinks, reportedly

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so these sounds are heard rather than spelt

parts.note: an inn is a pub and juices are fruit drinks

explanation.surface: Someone goes to buy orange juice at the local.
explanation.walkthrough: Said quickly, 'inn juices' runs together into a word that means persuades.
explanation.definitionFit: To get someone to do something is to persuade or bring them round to it, as in 'got him to sign'.

clue.text: Seat incorporating new electronic mechanism — it moves forward all by itself

definitions.text: it moves forward all by itself

indicators.note: to incorporate is to take something into one's body, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a chair is a seat
N is the standard abbreviation for new
E is short for electronic, as in e-mail
the action of a piano or gun is its working mechanism

explanation.surface: A description of a motorised seat that propels itself along.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: each step of the process triggers the next, so it keeps going without outside help.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-sustaining sequence of events, each causing the following one, proceeds without any further push from outside.

clue.text: Nun has pink champagne, finally stirred — not like Bond's martini

indicators.note: stirring mixes things up, so the letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of each word it governs

parts.note: the closing letters of both words

explanation.surface: A nun sips a stirred pink champagne cocktail, unlike James Bond who wants his drink prepared differently.
explanation.walkthrough: Bond famously orders his martini 'shaken, not stirred', so a drink not like his is the opposite. 'Stirred' neatly echoes that catchphrase while doing the jumbling.
explanation.definitionFit: Bond's vodka martini is always shaken, so anything unlike it has not been agitated in a cocktail shaker.

clue.text: Vindictiveness, eating last of partner's brownie

indicators.note: something eaten ends up inside the eater, so one piece is swallowed by the other

parts.note: spite is malicious vindictiveness

indicators.note: the last of a word is its closing letter alone

parts.note: the closing letter of the word, ignoring the apostrophe-s

explanation.surface: Out of spite, someone scoffs their partner's chocolate cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brownie' looks like the chocolate cake, but here it is the folklore creature: a brownie is a small household goblin.
explanation.definitionFit: In folklore a brownie is a helpful little goblin, one kind of fairy or elf creature.

clue.text: Following operation, this could set mine off

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
use is operation, as in 'in operation'

explanation.surface: After surgery, something might set my temper off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mine' reads as the possessive, but it is the explosive device.
explanation.definitionFit: A cord or device that detonates an explosive charge, such as a buried landmine, when lit or triggered.

clue.text: Every so often Auntie Ann's girls help in the kitchen, perhaps

indicators.note: something done every so often happens at intervals, so only letters at regular spacing count

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth letters and so on, running across the words

explanation.surface: From time to time Aunt Ann's daughters lend a hand with the cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: The girls really do sound like kitchen helpers, but the help is an object; 'perhaps' warns that the definition is by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A spoon or whisk is a tool used while cooking, so it is an aid in preparing food.

clue.text: State of cosy affluence? Yes, a setter's loaded

indicators.note: loaded is slang for drunk, and a drunk's words come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The crossword setter admits to being rich and comfortable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loaded' plausibly means wealthy, matching the surface, but it signals drunken scrambling; the 's is short for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Living on this road is an idiom for being comfortably well off, free of money worries.

clue.text: Backed plan limiting newspaperman's channels of communication

indicators.note: to limit is to set bounds around, so one piece encloses the other
something backed is moved back to front, so the word runs the other way

parts.note: an aim is a plan or intention
ED is short for editor, the newspaperman in charge

explanation.surface: A supported scheme restricts a journalist's lines of communication.
explanation.walkthrough: ED for editor is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Press, television and radio are the means by which news and information reach the public, collectively called this.

clue.text: Small lass with pert bust lacking obvious support

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as in clothing sizes

indicators.note: bust means broken, and broken things are reassembled differently

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cheeky description of a slim girl's figure and her lingerie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' fits the underwear picture perfectly, which hides that it means broken.
explanation.definitionFit: A dress or bra without shoulder bands has no visible means of holding it up.

clue.text: Freedom for art … as Browning got, when he and Lizzie tied the knot?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an artist's liberty to depart from fact or rules

definitions.text: as Browning got, when he and Lizzie tied the knot
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the marriage permit a famous Victorian writer of verse obtained

explanation.walkthrough: Robert Browning, the poet, married Elizabeth Barrett in 1846; a couple needs a licence to marry, so his was literally a poet's licence.
explanation.definitionFit: Writers and artists are allowed to bend facts or grammar for effect; this is the standard phrase for that liberty.

clue.text: They can rectify eye deficiencies? Nelson ecstatic, sadly having lost one

indicators.note: sadly means badly or in a sorry state, so the letters are in disorder
something lost is gone, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Admiral Nelson, famously blind in one eye, is overjoyed by a cure.
explanation.walkthrough: Nelson lost the sight of an eye in battle, so 'lost one' plausibly evokes him; it actually removes an I from the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Thin corrective discs worn on the eyeball correct short or long sight, like spectacles do.

clue.text: Subsequently presents enthralling paper on English king

indicators.note: to enthral is to hold captive, so one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: awards are presents or prizes
FT is the Financial Times newspaper
E is the abbreviation for English
R is for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Someone then hands out a captivating paper on an English monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means placed above, so the newspaper sits on top of the English king.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean at a later time, after the events just described.

clue.text: Bond producer comparatively quickly bringing in vacuous nymphette

indicators.note: bringing something in takes it inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: faster is the comparative of fast

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the word loses its middle and keeps its outside letters

parts.note: the first and last letters with the inside emptied

explanation.surface: A James Bond film-maker hurriedly casts a brainless starlet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bond producer' suggests a film mogul, but it is anything that creates a bond, a join between two things.
explanation.definitionFit: A clip, button or zip joins two things together, creating a physical link between them.

clue.text: Defending poorly, Gunners ending in heap around post

indicators.note: defenders surround what they protect, so one piece goes inside the other
to come around is to turn about, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: RA is the Royal Artillery, the army's gunners

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its closing letter alone

parts.note: the closing letter of the word
poorly means unwell

explanation.surface: Arsenal, nicknamed the Gunners, defend badly and end up with the ball in the net around the goalpost.
explanation.walkthrough: The Gunners is the nickname of Arsenal football club, which fits the surface, but crosswords use it for the Royal Artillery.
explanation.definitionFit: An upright column supporting a structure is an upright post.

clue.text: Prop in bar with lock

parts.note: bar means except, as does but: 'all bar one'
a tress is a lock of hair

explanation.surface: A rugby prop forward in a pub with a lock forward.
explanation.walkthrough: Prop and lock are both rugby positions, which the surface plays on; 'bar' is the preposition meaning except, not a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A projecting structure built against a wall to support it serves as a prop.

clue.text: Imagine former partner favoured cuddling Charlie

parts.note: an ex is a former partner

indicators.note: to cuddle is to wrap your arms around, so one piece embraces the other

parts.note: a pet is a favoured one, as in teacher's pet
Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Picture your old flame's favourite snuggling up to someone called Charlie.
explanation.walkthrough: PET as an adjective means favoured, like a pet project.
explanation.definitionFit: 'I imagine so' and 'I expect so' both mean suppose or think likely.

clue.text: When liquid, place in large beaker?

indicators.note: something liquid flows and has no fixed shape, so the letters take a new form

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Instructions to pour a liquid into a big laboratory vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: A beaker is lab glassware, but read as 'one with a beak' a large beaker is a big-billed bird; the question mark flags that pun.
explanation.definitionFit: This water bird has an enormous bill with a throat pouch, so it is something with a large beak.

clue.text: Plump young attendant taking half of spread?

parts.note: full as in full-figured, plump
a page is a boy attendant, as at a wedding

explanation.surface: A chubby pageboy helps himself to half the buffet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spread' looks like a meal, but it is a two-page spread in a newspaper or magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: A double-page magazine spread consists of two facing leaves, so an advert filling one side covers half.

clue.text: Certain wider US sanctions partially lifted

indicators.note: in a down clue lifting makes the letters read upwards, the other way round
partially means only in part, so just a stretch of the words is used

parts.note: a run of letters across the three words

explanation.surface: A news headline: Washington's broader embargo has been eased in part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifted' sounds like sanctions being removed, which is the surface, but it is the signal to read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sure or confident of an outcome is certain of it.

clue.text: Base metal American soldier used up making torch

indicators.note: in a down clue 'up' sends the letters upwards, so they read in reverse

parts.note: e is the base of natural logarithms
tin is a metal
a GI is a US soldier

explanation.surface: A US soldier makes a flashlight out of scrap metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base metal' looks like one phrase for a cheap metal; split it, and 'base' is the mathematical constant e.
explanation.definitionFit: To torch something is to set fire to it, so the verb means set alight.

clue.text: Spooner's secretly approaching DIY store for old-fashioned mobility aids

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so initial sounds trade places

parts.note: to stalk is to creep up on quarry unseen
Wickes is a British chain of DIY and building-supply shops

explanation.surface: Someone sneaks up on a hardware shop to buy old-style walking aids.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of STALKING WICKES and you get the answer; Wickes is a UK home-improvement chain.
explanation.definitionFit: Canes for leaning on while walking were the traditional way to help unsteady people get about.

clue.text: Pick up present for a listener

indicators.note: a listener takes in sounds, not spelling, so the word is judged by how it is spoken

parts.note: here means present, as when answering a roll call

explanation.surface: Collect a gift for someone who is listening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like a gift; it is the adjective, as in 'present and correct'.
explanation.definitionFit: To pick up a sound or a radio signal is to detect it with the ears.

clue.text: Obscure Colin Dexter novel — 50 put out, then 10

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are made into a new arrangement
something put out is ejected, so these letters are removed

parts.note: taken as written; Colin Dexter wrote the Inspector Morse novels
L is the Roman numeral 50
X is the Roman numeral 10

explanation.surface: A little-known detective book by the creator of Inspector Morse, described like a cricket scorecard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a noun naming one of Dexter's books; it is the adjective meaning new.
explanation.definitionFit: Knowledge that is little known or hard to understand is described as abstruse.

clue.text: Not once advancing rook is daring

indicators.note: to advance is to move forward, so this letter leaves its place and slots in earlier

parts.note: never means not at any time, not once
R is the chess notation for rook

explanation.surface: A chess commentary: pushing the rook forward is never a bold move.
explanation.walkthrough: The R at the end of NEVER moves up one place, as a chess piece advances.
explanation.definitionFit: Daring as a noun means boldness or courage, the quality of having the guts to act.

clue.text: Decline contract, ignoring HR

indicators.note: to ignore something is to leave it out, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: to contract is to get smaller
taken as written

explanation.surface: An employee turns down a job contract without involving the personnel department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decline' and 'contract' both look like an office scene; both are verbs meaning go down and get smaller. HR is human resources.
explanation.definitionFit: To decline in value or strength is to fall or drop lower.

clue.text: She brings us the latest mobile — we are nerds!

indicators.note: mobile means able to move about, so the letters shift around

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A tech enthusiast celebrates the woman who sells them the newest phone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The latest mobile' reads as the newest phone; 'the latest' belongs to the definition and 'mobile' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A presenter on radio or television reads out current events, so she delivers the most recent news.
